q-81734.name: Question 1
q-81734.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2{x}^{2}y+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}y+{g}^{′}(y) & =2{x}^{2}y+1 \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =1 \\ g(y) & =y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}+x+y+C.
$$

Question 1
?

Find f(x,y) such that ∇f=F, where F(x,y)=(2xy2+1)i+(2x2y+1)j.

a
f(x,y)=4xy+xy+C
b
f(x,y)=x2y2+y+C
c
f(x,y)=x2y2+x+y+C
d
f(x,y)=2x2y2+C
e
f(x,y)=2x2y2+x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2xy2+1,∂f∂y=2x2y+1

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(2xy2+1)dx=x2y2+x+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=2x2y+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=2x2y+1 into account, we obtain 2x2y+g′(y)=2x2y+1g′(y)=1g(y)=y+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=y+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=x2y2+x+y+C.

q-81738.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y)=F(x,y),$ the function $f(x,y)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4-2xy
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}-x{y}^{2}+g(y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-2xy+{g}^{′}(y).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=4-2xy$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2xy+{g}^{′}(y) & =4-2xy \\ {g}^{′}(y) & =4 \\ g(y) & =4y+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Finally, substituting $g(y)=4y+C$ into our expression for $f(x,y),$ we get

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}-x{y}^{2}+4y+C.
$$

a

b

EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y) is defined as ∇f(x,y)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj.

Since ∇f(x,y)=F(x,y), the function f(x,y) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=3x2−y2,∂f∂y=4−2xy

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y: f(x,y)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(3x2−y2)dx=x3−xy2+g(y)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain

∂f∂y=−2xy+g′(y).

Taking ∂f∂y=4−2xy into account, we obtain −2xy+g′(y)=4−2xyg′(y)=4g(y)=4y+C, where C is a constant.

Finally, substituting g(y)=4y+C into our expression for f(x,y), we get f(x,y)=x3−xy2+4y+C.

q-124733.name: Question 3
q-124733.problem:
Consider the function

$$
F(x,y,z)=({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,i+2xy{z}^{3}\,j+(3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z})\,k.
$$

Find $f(x,y,z)$ such that $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).$
q-124733.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({y}^{2}{z}^{3}-{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2xy{z}^{3}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy{z}^{3}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =2xy{z}^{3} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int 0\,\text{d}y \\  & =h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) & =3x{y}^{2}{z}^{2}-x{e}^{z} \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}{z}^{3}-x{e}^{z}+C.
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the function F(x,y,z)=(y2z3−ez)i+2xyz3j+(3xy2z2−xez)k. Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z).

a
 f(x,y,z)=xyz−yez+C
b
 f(x,y,z)=xy2z3−xez+C
c
 f(x,y,z)=x3y2+xz−ez+C
d
 f(x,y,z)=y3z−xez+C
e
 f(x,y,z)=xy2z3+yz−ez+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=y2z3−ez,∂f∂y=2xyz3,∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(y2z3−ez)dx=xy2z3−xez+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=2xyz3+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=2xyz3 into account, we obtain 2xyz3+∂g∂y=2xyz3∂g∂y=0

Now we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫0dy=h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=xy2z3−xez+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=3xy2z2−xez into account, we obtain 3xy2z2−xez+h′(z)=3xy2z2−xezh′(z)=0h(z)=C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=xy2z3−xez+C.

q-132100.name: Question 4
q-132100.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\operatorname{ln}⁡y+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{y}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{x}{y}-{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =-{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int (-{z}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =-y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=-y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=-2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-2yz & =-2yz+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =0 \\ h(z) & =C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x-y{z}^{2}+C.
$$

q-132103.worked_solution:
The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,k.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y{e}^{z},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1,\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2x+y{e}^{z})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x{e}^{z}+1$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{z}+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =x{e}^{z}+1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int \,\text{d}y \\  & =y+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+xy{e}^{z}+y+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}=xy{e}^{z}-2z$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}xy{e}^{z}-2z & =xy{e}^{z}+{h}^{′}(z) \\ {h}^{′}(z) & =-2z \\ h(z) & =-{z}^{2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Consequently,

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy{e}^{z}+{x}^{2}+y-{z}^{2}+C.
$$

Question 5
?

Find f(x,y,z) such that ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), where F(x,y,z)=(2x+yez)i+(xez+1)j+(xyez−2z)k.

a
 f(x,y,z)=xyzez+x+y−z2+C
b
 f(x,y,z)=xez+yx2+x−z2+C
c
 f(x,y,z)=xyez+x+y−z+C
d
 f(x,y,z)=xyez+x2+x+y2z+C
e
f(x,y,z)=xyez+x2+y−z2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the function f(x,y,z) is defined as ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂xi+∂f∂yj+∂f∂zk.

Since ∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z), the function f(x,y,z) must satisfy the following system: ∂f∂x=2x+yez,∂f∂y=xez+1,∂f∂z=xyez−2z

First, we integrate ∂f∂x with respect to x. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of y and z: f(x,y,z)=∫∂f∂xdx=∫(2x+yez)dx=x2+xyez+g(y,z)

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to y, we obtain ∂f∂y=xez+∂g∂y

Taking ∂f∂y=xez+1 into account, we obtain

xez+∂g∂y=xez+1∂g∂y=1

Now, we integrate ∂g∂y with respect to y. Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of z: g(y,z)=∫∂g∂ydy=∫dy=y+h(z)

Substituting g(y,z)=y+h(z) in the expression for f(x,y,z), we get f(x,y,z)=x2+xyez+y+h(z).

To determine the function h(z), we differentiate f(x,y,z) with respect to z. This gives ∂f∂z=xyez+h′(z).

Taking ∂f∂z=xyez−2z into account, we obtain xyez−2z=xyez+h′(z)h′(z)=−2zh(z)=−z2+C, where C is a constant.

Consequently, f(x,y,z)=xyez+x2+y−z2+C.
